![Spectrum of shared metacognition, from intrinsic (agent runs its own metacognitive loop) through shared (agent and designer split the metacognitive work) to extrinsic (metacognitive loop is fully externally defined). Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.png){fig-align="center"}

In *Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning* (ICML 2025) [[1]](#ref-1), [Tennison Liu](https://tennisonliu.github.io/) and [Mihaela van der Schaar](https://www.vanderschaar-lab.com/prof-mihaela-van-der-schaar/) at Cambridge argue that almost every current "self-improving" LLM agent leans on hand-designed metacognitive loops, and that genuine, sustained self-improvement requires agents that can themselves evaluate, plan, and adapt their own learning processes.

> Self-improving agents aim to continuously acquire new capabilities with minimal supervision. However, current approaches face two key limitations: their self-improvement processes are often rigid, fail to generalize across tasks domains, and struggle to scale with increasing agent capabilities. We argue that *effective self-improvement requires intrinsic metacognitive learning, defined as an agent's intrinsic ability to actively evaluate, reflect on, and adapt its own learning processes*. Drawing inspiration from human metacognition, we introduce a formal framework comprising three components: *metacognitive knowledge* (self-assessment of capabilities, tasks, and learning strategies), *metacognitive planning* (deciding what and how to learn), and *metacognitive evaluation* (reflecting on learning experiences to improve future learning). Analyzing existing self-improving agents, we find they *rely predominantly on extrinsic metacognitive mechanisms, which are fixed, human-designed loops that limit scalability and adaptability*. Examining each component, we contend that many ingredients for intrinsic metacognition are already present. Finally, we explore how to optimally distribute metacognitive responsibilities between humans and agents, and robustly evaluate and improve intrinsic metacognitive learning, key challenges that must be addressed to enable truly sustained, generalized, and aligned self-improvement.

## Method

The paper lays out a three-component framework for metacognitive learning. *Metacognitive knowledge* is the agent's self-assessment of its own capabilities and the tasks it faces. *Metacognitive planning* is deciding what to learn and how to go about it. *Metacognitive evaluation* is reflecting on learning outcomes to improve future learning.

## Results

The paper walks three well-known systems through this framework as case studies, ordered by increasing intrinsic-ness:

- **STaR** [[4]](#ref-4) (Zelikman et al., 2022): a reasoning bootstrapping method. Given a small set of problems with reasoning traces plus a larger set with answers only, the agent attempts problems and gets finetuned on any trace that led to a correct answer, then the cycle repeats on harder problems. Almost entirely extrinsic: the agent doesn't assess its own capabilities, doesn't choose which tasks to attempt (externally curated), and doesn't adapt its learning strategy (rationalization with answer hints is fixed). The metacognitive loop sits with the system designer.
- **Voyager** (Wang et al., 2023): an LLM-based embodied agent for lifelong learning in Minecraft. It maintains a growing library of executable Python skills and autonomously discovers increasingly complex actions to perform. Partially intrinsic: the agent tracks what it can do (knowledge) and balances exploration against task learnability when picking next goals (planning). The learning strategy stays fixed though: the same exploration-learning loop runs across all tasks. Voyager beats expert-designed curriculum baselines, which the paper takes as evidence the intrinsic components matter.
- **Generative Agents** (Park et al., 2023): agents in a Sims-style sandbox that accumulate experiences, form relationships, and develop distinct personas through lived interaction. Most intrinsic of the three. Agents form evolving identities and motivations (knowledge), autonomously plan daily activities (planning), and periodically trigger an abstract reflection, such as recognizing a newfound interest or reinterpreting recent events, that updates their semantic memory and shapes future plans (evaluation). The paper flags the contrast with Reflexion-style techniques: Reflexion reflects at the cognitive level to improve performance on specific tasks; Generative Agents reflect at the metacognitive level, drawing inferences about their own trajectory.

The arc across the three case studies is how the paper builds its argument: each system is intrinsic on more components than the last, and the paper argues the more-intrinsic systems show more sustained progress in the diversity and novelty of their evolving capabilities. The paper acknowledges these are preliminary observations that still require rigorous, systematic studies to substantiate.

## My Notes

- **The paper's two foundational claims each lean on one piece of support.** Static self-improvement loops, the authors argue, have two problems: they fail to generalize across domains, and they lose efficacy as agents get stronger. The "lose efficacy" claim cites one empirical study, Song et al.'s 2024 generation-verification-gap finding [[6]](#ref-6). The "fail to generalize" claim points at existing systems (STaR, bootstrapped self-training) that worked in their original domain but haven't transferred. No new experiments are presented.

- **The intrinsic vs. extrinsic distinction is a sharper way to read recent agent work.** Most public discussion of "self-improving agents" treats the term as binary (does the agent get better over time, yes or no). This paper asks a sharper question: *who decided what gets monitored, what counts as progress, and when to switch strategies?* In nearly every shipped agentic system today, those answers are wired in by the system designer. Two recent examples make the point cleanly: [Supervising Ralph Wiggum](/posts/20260430-supervising-ralph-wiggum/) [[2]](#ref-2) hand-designs a Co-Regulation Agent whose role and loop position are fixed, and [ReMA](/posts/20260430-rema-meta-think/) [[3]](#ref-3) hand-designs the high-low decomposition and trains policies for it. Both work; both are extrinsic in this paper's taxonomy. The same critique applies to the prompt-optimization literature: [MASS](/posts/20260430-multi-agent-system-search/), [MetaSPO](/posts/20260430-metaspo-system-prompt-meta-learning/), and [EvoPrompt](/posts/20260430-evoprompt/) all use LLMs as inner-loop optimizers but the search-space structure (what to optimize, in what order, against what objective) is fixed by humans.

- **The framework labels but doesn't predict.** Walking STaR [[4]](#ref-4) through the three components shows exactly which parts are agent-driven and which are designer-driven, which is more useful than saying it "doesn't generalize." But since every current system lands in the extrinsic category, the framework doesn't distinguish extrinsic designs that will hit a wall soon from designs with a lot of headroom. The paper raises the harder question of which extrinsic shortcuts will collapse first as agent capabilities grow, but doesn't answer it.

- **The "sustained progress" trend claim stays qualitative because the three domains don't share a common measurement.** The systems live in incomparable domains: math/reasoning for STaR, Minecraft for Voyager, Sims-style simulation for Generative Agents. No shared benchmark means no single metric to plot. You can get partway toward a domain-agnostic metric by looking at shape properties of each system's own learning curve, like the slope late in training normalized by slope early (a residual learning rate), which is unit-free on the y-axis. But the x-axis is still domain-specific: one training step of STaR isn't one training step of Voyager, and there's no canonical way to align Sims days with Minecraft exploration steps. Substantiating the cross-system ordering would need either a shared benchmark or a principled way to align per-system x-axes, neither of which the paper provides.

- **The "many ingredients are already present" claim is the optimistic bet and the most testable.** The paper argues that frontier LLMs already exhibit pieces of metacognitive knowledge (awareness of their own capabilities and task demands), planning (strategy selection), and evaluation (progress tracking and self-critique). The implicit prediction is that an architecture which lets the agent compose these capabilities into its own meta-loop, rather than baking the loop in at design time, should outperform extrinsic baselines on tasks where the right meta-strategy is itself unknown. Empirical work has already started bounding what those "ingredients" can do unaided: Apple's [SelfReflect](/posts/20260430-selfreflect-internal-distribution/) [[5]](#ref-5) shows that LLM self-reports of their own answer distributions do not match the distributions those models actually sample from, across 20 modern models. The metacognitive-knowledge ingredient, at least the facet SelfReflect bounds (the ability to faithfully describe one's own answer distribution), is thinner than the position paper's optimism implies, at least without scaffolding like sample-then-summarize.
